facts.text: Whoever loads and secures the cargo, you are responsible for inspecting your cargo.
You are responsible for recognizing an overload and badly balanced weight.
You are responsible for knowing that your cargo is secured and does not block your view ahead or to the sides.
You are responsible for knowing that your cargo does not block your way to the emergency equipment.
Loose cargo that falls off can cause a crash, and it can hurt or kill you in a quick stop. An overload can damage the vehicle and make steering harder.
To carry hazardous material that needs placards you also need a hazardous materials endorsement.

cards.q: What four cargo duties are yours, whoever loaded it?
cards.a: Inspect the cargo, spot overloads and bad balance, secure it and keep your view clear, and keep emergency equipment reachable.

cards.q: What do you need to haul placarded hazardous material?
cards.a: A hazardous materials endorsement.

exam.q: Someone else loaded and secured your trailer. Who is responsible for the load?
exam.why: Whoever loads it, the driver is responsible for inspecting it, spotting overloads, and securing it.

reading.p: You must understand the basic cargo safety rules to get a CDL, whether or not you load the vehicle yourself.

ul: Loose cargo that falls off causes traffic trouble, and it can hurt or kill somebody.
Loose cargo inside can hurt or kill you in a quick stop or a crash.
An overload can damage your vehicle.
How the vehicle is loaded changes the steering, and a bad load is harder to control.

reading.h: Four things that are yours, whoever loaded it

ul: Inspecting your cargo.
Recognizing an overload and badly balanced weight.
Knowing the cargo is secured and does not block your view ahead or to the sides.
Knowing the cargo does not block your way to the emergency equipment.

reading.note: To carry hazardous material that needs placards you also need a hazardous materials endorsement.

facts.text: Inspect the cargo and its securing devices again within the first 50 miles of a trip, and make any adjustment needed.
Inspect the cargo again after every three hours or 150 miles of driving.
Inspect the cargo again after every break you take while driving.
Rules for weight, securing cargo, covering loads and where a large vehicle may drive differ from place to place, so know the rules where you drive.

cards.q: When is the first cargo re-inspection after you set off?
cards.a: Within the first 50 miles.

cards.q: How often must you re-inspect cargo while driving?
cards.a: Every 3 hours or 150 miles, and after every break.

exam.q: How soon after starting a trip must you inspect your cargo again?
exam.why: The first re-inspection is within 50 miles, then every 3 hours or 150 miles and after each break.

exam.q: You have driven 150 miles since your last cargo check. What must you do?
choices: Inspect the cargo and its securing devices
exam.why: Cargo is re-inspected after 3 hours or 150 miles of driving, whichever comes first.

reading.p: Check the load as part of your vehicle inspection: not overloaded, balanced, and secured. Then check it again on the road.

numbers.what: the first re-check, after you start the trip
then re-check again, whichever comes first
re-check after each break you take while driving

reading.note: Re-check as often as you need to keep the load secure. Those numbers are the minimum, not the target.

reading.p: Rules for weight, securing cargo, covering loads and where a large vehicle may drive change from place to place. Know the rules where you will drive.
You are responsible for not being overloaded. To do that, you need the weight words the rules use.

facts.text: Gross vehicle weight rating, the GVWR, is the loaded weight of a single vehicle, as the maker specifies it.
Gross combination weight rating, the GCWR, is the maker's value for the power unit, or the sum of the ratings or weights of the power unit and the towed units that gives the highest value.
Axle weight is the weight that one axle, or one set of axles, puts on the ground.
Tire load is the most weight a tire can carry safely at a stated pressure, and the rating is written on the side of the tire.
A suspension system has a weight capacity rating from its maker, and a coupling device is rated for the most weight it can pull or carry.

cards.q: What is GVWR?
cards.a: The maker's loaded weight for a single vehicle.

cards.q: What is GCWR?
cards.a: The maker's rating for the power unit, or the combined ratings of the power unit and towed units, whichever is highest.

cards.q: What is axle weight?
cards.a: The weight one axle or set of axles puts on the ground.

cards.q: Where is the tire load rating written?
cards.a: On the side of each tire.

exam.q: Where do you find the maximum safe weight a tire can carry?
choices: On the side of the tire
exam.why: The tire load rating is stated on the side of each tire, at a specified pressure.

numbers.what: gross vehicle weight rating: the maker's loaded weight for a single vehicle
gross combination weight rating: the maker's value for the power unit, or the combined ratings or weights of power unit and towed units, whichever is highest
the weight one axle, or one set of axles, puts on the ground
the most weight a tire can carry safely at a stated pressure

reading.note: The tire load rating is written on the side of each tire.

reading.p: A suspension system has a weight capacity rating from its maker. A coupling device is rated for the most weight it can pull or carry.

facts.text: A bridge formula often sets the maximum axle weights, and it allows less weight on axles that are closer together, to protect bridges and roads.
Overloading hurts steering, braking and speed control. Stopping distance grows, and brakes can fail when they work too hard.
An overloaded truck crawls up a grade and can gain too much speed going down.
In bad weather or in the mountains it may be unsafe to run at the legal maximum weight, so think about that before you drive.

cards.q: What does a bridge formula do?
cards.a: It sets lower maximum axle weights for axles that are closer together.

cards.q: Name two times when legal maximum weight may not be safe.
cards.a: Bad weather and mountain driving.

cards.q: What does overloading do to your brakes?
cards.a: Stopping distance grows, and the brakes can fail from working too hard.

exam.q: When might a legal maximum weight still be unsafe?
choices: In bad weather or in the mountains
exam.why: Bad weather and mountain driving can make legal maximum weights unsafe.

reading.p: States set maximums for gross vehicle weight ratings, gross combination weight ratings and axle weights. You must stay inside them.
Maximum axle weights often come from a bridge formula, which allows less weight on axles that sit closer together. That keeps bridges and roadways from being overloaded.

ul: It hurts steering, braking and speed control.
It makes you crawl up a grade, and worse, it can let you gain too much speed going down.
It lengthens your stopping distance.
It can make the brakes fail, because they are forced to work too hard.

reading.note: In bad weather or in the mountains, even a legal maximum weight may not be safe. Think about it before you drive.

facts.text: A high center of gravity, from cargo piled high or heavy cargo on top, makes a rollover more likely, and the danger is worst in a curve or a swerve.
Spread the cargo as low as you can, and put the heaviest parts under the lightest parts.

cards.q: What does a high center of gravity do?
cards.a: It makes the vehicle more likely to tip over, above all in curves or a swerve.

cards.q: Where do the heaviest parts of the load go?
cards.a: Under the lightest parts, as low as possible.

exam.q: Where should the heaviest part of a load be placed?
exam.why: Keep the center of gravity low: the heaviest parts go under the lightest parts.

reading.p: The height of the center of gravity decides how the vehicle handles. Pile the cargo high, or put the heavy cargo on top, and the center of gravity goes up with it.

reading.note: A high center of gravity makes a rollover more likely, and the danger is worst in a curve or when you swerve to miss something.

reading.p: Spread the load as low as you can, and put the heaviest parts under the lightest parts.

facts.text: Too much weight on the steering axle makes steering hard, and it can damage the steering axle and the tires.
An under-loaded front axle, from weight pushed too far back, makes the steering axle too light to steer safely.
Too little weight on the driving axles gives poor traction, and the drive wheels spin easily in bad weather.
On a flat bed there is also a greater chance that a high load will shift sideways or fall off.

cards.q: What does too much weight on the steering axle cause?
cards.a: Hard steering, and damage to the steering axle and tires.

cards.q: What happens with too little weight on the front axle?
cards.a: The steering axle gets too light to steer safely.

cards.q: What happens with too little weight on the drive axles?
cards.a: Poor traction, and the drive wheels spin easily.

exam.q: Weight is loaded too far to the rear. What is the result?
choices: The steering axle gets too light to steer safely
exam.why: An under-loaded front axle makes the steering axle too light to steer safely.

reading.p: Where the weight sits matters as much as how much there is.

ul: Too much weight on the steering axle: hard steering, and damage to the axle and tires.
Too little weight on the front axle, from weight pushed too far back: the steering axle gets too light to steer safely.
Too little weight on the driving axles: poor traction, and the drive wheels spin easily. In bad weather the truck may not keep going.
Weight too high: a greater chance of rollover, and on a flat bed a greater chance the load shifts sideways or falls off.

reading.p: Cargo must be held in place. There are three ways to do it, and they work together: blocking, bracing and tie-downs.

facts.text: Blocking goes at the front, the back and the sides of the cargo to stop it sliding, and it is shaped to fit the cargo snugly and fixed to the deck.
Bracing runs from the upper part of the cargo to the floor or the walls of the cargo compartment, to stop the cargo moving.

cards.q: What is blocking?
cards.a: Shaped material at the front, back or sides of cargo, fixed to the deck, to stop it sliding.

cards.q: What is bracing?
cards.a: Support from the upper part of the cargo down to the floor or walls.

ul: Blocking goes at the front, the back and the sides of the cargo, to stop it sliding. It is shaped to fit the cargo snugly and fixed to the cargo deck.
Bracing runs from the upper part of the cargo down to the floor or the walls of the cargo compartment, to stop the cargo moving.

facts.text: A securement system's total working load limit must be at least one half the weight of the article or group of articles it holds.
Cargo needs at least one tie-down for every ten feet of cargo.
However small the cargo is, it needs at least two tie-downs.
Tie-downs must be the right type and strength, and they must be attached to the vehicle correctly, by hooks, bolts, rails or rings.
Heavy metal pieces have special securing requirements, so find out what they are before you carry such a load.

cards.q: How many tie-downs per length of cargo?
cards.a: At least one for every ten feet.

cards.q: What is the minimum number of tie-downs for any load?
cards.a: Two, however small the cargo is.

cards.q: How many tie-downs for a 20-foot load?
cards.a: Two.

cards.q: How strong must a securement system be?
cards.a: Its total working load limit must be at least half the weight of the cargo.

exam.q: What is the least number of tie-downs for any flatbed load?
exam.why: Two tie-downs at least, however small the cargo, and one more for every ten feet.

exam.q: How many tie-downs does a 30-foot load need?
exam.why: One tie-down for every ten feet gives three for a 30-foot load.

exam.q: A securement system must have a total working load limit of at least:
choices: One quarter of the cargo weight
One half of the cargo weight
exam.why: Federal rules require at least one half the weight of the article or group of articles.

reading.p: On a flatbed, or a trailer with no sides, the cargo must be tied down so it cannot shift or fall off. In a closed van, tie-downs still matter, because shifting cargo changes how the vehicle handles.

numbers.what: the least total working load limit of the securement system, as a share of the cargo weight
the least number of tie-downs, by cargo length
the least number of tie-downs for any load, however small

reading.p: A 20-foot load needs two tie-downs. A 30-foot load needs three.

reading.note: Use the proper equipment: ropes, straps, chains, and tensioning devices such as winches, ratchets and clinching components. Attach them to the vehicle correctly, by hooks, bolts, rails or rings.

reading.p: Heavy pieces of metal have special securing requirements. Find out what they are before you carry such a load.

facts.text: A front-end header board, also called a headache rack, protects you from your cargo in a crash or a hard stop, and it must block the cargo moving forward.

cards.q: What does a header board do?
cards.a: It blocks cargo from moving forward and protects the driver in a crash or hard stop.

reading.p: A front-end header board, which drivers call a headache rack, stands between you and the cargo. It protects you in a crash or an emergency stop.

reading.note: Make sure the front-end structure is in good condition, and that it will block your cargo from moving forward.

facts.text: There are two reasons to cover cargo: to protect people from spilled cargo, and to protect the cargo from the weather.
Spill protection is a safety requirement in many states, so know the law where you drive.
Look at your cargo covers in the mirrors from time to time, because a flapping cover can tear loose, uncover the cargo and block your view or another driver's.

cards.q: What are the two reasons for covering cargo?
cards.a: To protect people from spilled cargo, and to protect the cargo from weather.

cards.q: Why watch your cargo cover in the mirrors?
cards.a: A flapping cover can tear loose and block your view or someone else's.

exam.q: What are the two basic reasons for covering cargo?
exam.why: Cover cargo to protect people from spills and to protect the cargo from weather.

ul: To protect people from spilled cargo.
To protect the cargo from the weather.

reading.p: Spill protection is a safety requirement in many states. Know the law where you drive.

reading.note: Look at the cargo covers in your mirrors from time to time. A flapping cover can tear loose, uncover the cargo, and block your view or another driver's.

facts.text: You cannot inspect a sealed load, but you must still check that you are inside the gross weight and axle weight limits.
A container must be secured like any other cargo, whether it locks into a special frame or sits on a flatbed trailer.

cards.q: What must you check on a sealed load?
cards.a: That you are within the gross weight and axle weight limits.

exam.q: You carry a sealed container you cannot inspect. What must you still check?
choices: Gross weight and axle weight limits
exam.why: A sealed load cannot be inspected inside, but the weight limits are still yours to check.

reading.p: A containerized load is usually freight that travels part of the way by rail or ship, with a truck at one or both ends. Some containers lock into a special frame. Others sit on a flatbed trailer, and they must be secured like any other cargo.

reading.note: You cannot inspect a sealed load. You must still check that you are inside the gross weight and the axle weight limits.

reading.p: Some loads behave badly even when they are secured properly. These four need extra care.

facts.text: A dry bulk tank has a high center of gravity and the load can shift, so go slowly and carefully through curves and sharp turns.

cards.q: Why do dry bulk tanks need special care?
cards.a: High center of gravity and a load that can shift. Go slowly in curves and sharp turns.

reading.p: A dry bulk tank carries a high center of gravity, and the load can shift inside.

reading.note: Be slow and careful through curves and sharp turns.

facts.text: Hanging meat is an unstable load with a high center of gravity, so take special care and go slowly on sharp curves such as on-ramps and off-ramps.

cards.q: Why is hanging meat a difficult load?
cards.a: It is unstable with a high center of gravity, so ramps and sharp curves need slow speed.

reading.p: Hanging meat, which is suspended beef, pork or lamb in a refrigerated truck, is a very unstable load with a high center of gravity.

reading.note: Take particular care on sharp curves such as on-ramps and off-ramps. Go slowly.

facts.text: Livestock can move around and make handling unsafe. With less than a full load, use false bulkheads to keep the animals bunched together.
Even bunched together, livestock can lean on a curve, which shifts the center of gravity and makes a rollover more likely.

cards.q: How do you carry a part load of livestock?
cards.a: Use false bulkheads to keep the animals bunched together.

cards.q: Why is livestock still risky when bunched?
cards.a: The animals lean in curves, which shifts the center of gravity.

exam.q: You have a part load of livestock. What do you use?
choices: False bulkheads to bunch the animals
exam.why: False bulkheads keep livestock bunched so they cannot move about the trailer.

reading.p: Livestock move around in the trailer, and that makes handling unsafe.

ul: With less than a full load, use false bulkheads to keep the animals bunched together.
Even bunched, take special care: animals lean on a curve, which shifts the center of gravity and makes a rollover more likely.

facts.text: An over-length, over-width or overweight load needs a special transit permit, and driving is usually allowed only at certain times.
An oversized load may need wide load signs, flashing lights and flags, and it may need a police escort or pilot vehicles.

cards.q: What does an oversized load need?
cards.a: A special transit permit, limited driving hours, and often signs, lights, flags or an escort.

reading.p: A load that is over-length, over-width or overweight needs a special transit permit, and driving is usually limited to certain times.

ul: Special equipment may be needed, such as wide load signs, flashing lights and flags.
The load may need a police escort, or pilot vehicles with warning signs or flashing lights.

reading.note: These loads need special driving care.
